unit.title: Photosynthesis and Transport in Plants
unit.blurb: How plants make glucose by photosynthesis, how leaves are adapted for it, testing a leaf for starch, and how water and mineral salts travel from roots to leaves.

O1.t: Describe photosynthesis using its word equation and explain where the energy in food chains comes from.

O2.t: Describe how leaves and chloroplasts are adapted for photosynthesis and test a leaf for starch.

O3.t: Explain why plants need water, nitrates and magnesium.

O4.t: Describe how root hairs absorb water and how xylem and transpiration move water up a plant.

captions: Welcome to Camday.
This lesson was written by the Camday teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Stage 9, Unit 1: Photosynthesis and Transport in Plants.
Deforestation is destroying forests full of life.
Plants are producers: they make their own food by photosynthesis,
which uses carbon dioxide.
So how does cutting down trees affect us, besides reducing our food supply?
Plants make their own food by photosynthesis.
They use energy from light to turn carbon dioxide from
the air and water from the soil into glucose,
a sugar, and oxygen.
We can summarise it with a word equation: carbon dioxide plus water,
in the presence of light and chlorophyll, makes glucose plus oxygen.
'Photo' means from light, and 'synthesis' means putting together.
The glucose lets plants form new cells and tissues, which we call biomass.
Two pieces of pondweed are placed in water.
One lamp is 10 centimetres away from the first beaker;
another lamp is 50 centimetres away from the second.
Predict: which pondweed will give off more bubbles of gas?
Pause and decide.
Watch. Bubbles start to rise from both pieces of pondweed.
The pondweed close to the lamp gives off about 40 bubbles a minute;
the one far away gives off only about 6.
Explain what you saw.
The bubbles are oxygen, made by photosynthesis.
The closer lamp gives the pondweed more light energy,
so it photosynthesises faster and makes more oxygen.
Light is needed for photosynthesis, and more light means a faster rate,
up to a limit.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
A student counts the bubbles given off by pondweed in one minute,
with the lamp at five different distances.
At 10 centimetres there are 40 bubbles a minute.
At 20 centimetres there are 26, and at 30 centimetres, 15.
The further away the lamp, the fewer the bubbles,
but the line is a curve, not a straight line.
Pause and decide: what is the independent variable,
and why should the student keep the water temperature the same?
Plants are well adapted for photosynthesis.
Leaves have a large surface area to capture sunlight, and they're thin,
so gases diffuse in and out quickly.
Tiny openings called stomata, mostly on the underside of leaves,
let gases in and out.
Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll that absorbs light.
Root hairs give roots a huge surface area for absorbing water.
Some oxygen is used for respiration; the rest escapes through the stomata.
Glucose gives the plant energy, and extra glucose is stored as starch,
in leaves, roots, stems and fruits.
So the energy in every food chain comes from the Sun!
If a leaf has photosynthesised, it contains starch.
To test it, boil the leaf in water to stop all reactions,
then in ethanol, heated in hot water, to remove the green chlorophyll.
Careful: ethanol is flammable!
Then soften the leaf in hot water.
Add a few drops of iodine solution.
Iodine is normally brown, but turns blue-black when starch is present.
Keep a plant in the dark for 48 hours so it uses up its starch.
Cover half a leaf with black paper and put the plant in bright sunlight.
Only the uncovered half turns blue-black, showing that photosynthesis needs light.

rubric.pt: States a testable hypothesis linking carbon dioxide to the rate of photosynthesis
Changes the mass or concentration of sodium hydrogencarbonate
Measures the rate, e.g. bubbles per minute or volume of oxygen
Controls light intensity (lamp distance), temperature and the piece of pondweed
Repeats and calculates a mean

adv.model: My hypothesis is that the more carbon dioxide there is in the water, the faster the pondweed photosynthesises. I will change the mass of sodium hydrogencarbonate dissolved in the water, using 0 g, 1 g, 2 g and 3 g in the same volume. I will measure the rate by counting the bubbles of oxygen released in one minute. The lamp will stay at the same distance, and I will use the same piece of pondweed at the same temperature. I will repeat each count three times and calculate a mean. If the number of bubbles rises as the mass increases, the results support the hypothesis.

adv.prompt: * Advanced. SAPS suggests measuring the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed either by counting bubbles or by collecting the gas and measuring its volume. Evaluate which method gives more reliable results.

rubric.pt: bubbles can be different sizes, so counting is less accurate
collecting gas and measuring volume is more accurate / measures the total amount
repeat and take a mean / control temperature and CO₂

adv.model: Counting bubbles is quick, but bubbles are different sizes and can be missed, so it is less accurate. Collecting the gas in a syringe or measuring cylinder and measuring its volume measures the total amount of oxygen, so it is more reliable. Either way, each reading should be repeated and a mean taken, with the temperature kept the same.

captions: Water is vital for plants.
It carries dissolved mineral salts, it's a raw material for photosynthesis,
it helps control temperature through transpiration, and seeds need it to germinate.
Water also keeps plant cells firm.
When water fills the vacuole, it pushes against the cell wall,
making the cell turgid.
Without enough water, the cell becomes flaccid and the plant wilts.
Plants also need mineral salts.
Nitrates are used to make proteins and chlorophyll, and magnesium to make chlorophyll.
Without nitrates, leaves turn pale or yellow, so farmers add fertilisers.
A stalk of celery with leaves stands in water coloured with red food colouring,
for one day. Predict: where will the red colour end up?
Pause and decide.
Watch. After a few hours, the red colour starts to climb up the stalk.
After a day the leaves have red veins.
When the stalk is cut across,
the red shows up only as a ring of small dots.
Explain what you saw.
The red water travelled up the stalk in the xylem vessels,
the tubes that carry water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves.
Water evaporating from the leaves, transpiration, pulls more water up behind it.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Roots anchor the plant and absorb water.
Tiny root hairs give a huge surface area.
Water moves into root hair cells when the soil
has a higher water concentration than the cells,
carrying dissolved mineral salts like nitrates and magnesium with it.
Water and mineral salts travel up the plant in the xylem.
Xylem vessels are made of dead cells that have lost their contents and end walls,
forming long hollow tubes with thick, stiff walls.
What pulls the water up?
Transpiration: water evaporates in the leaves and escapes through the stomata,
pulling more water up the xylem, like drinking through a straw.
Now it is your turn to shine!

Question 1: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.

Question 2: What colour does iodine turn if starch is present?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Blue-black.
Question 3: Why do plants need nitrates?
Pause the video now.
Answer: To make proteins and chlorophyll.
Question 4: Which tissue carries water up a plant,
and what process pulls it?
Pause the video now.
Answer: The xylem, pulled by transpiration.
